title: Impact of Stimulated Brillouin Scattering on Modulation Instability in Fiber Fabry-Perot Resonators
authors: Alice Houard, Thomas Bunel, Matteo Conforti, Saliya Coulibaly, Arnaud Mussot
abstract: We report the experimental and numerical demonstration of stimulated Brillouin scattering-induced stabilization of Kerr-driven modulation instability in fiber Fabry--Perot resonators. We show that Brillouin scattering shapes the modulation instability spectrum into a stable multi--free-spectral-range cascade that is otherwise unstable in the absence of Brillouin effects. We further identify that this stabilization originates from the real part of the Brillouin response, leading to an asymmetric Kerr-Brillouin interaction governed by the relative position of the Brillouin frequency shift with respect to the cavity resonances. These results establish stimulated Brillouin scattering as an additional degree of freedom for controlling nonlinear dynamics in Kerr resonators.
summary: This research demonstrates that Stimulated Brillouin Scattering can stabilize modulation instability in optical fiber resonators. By incorporating SBS into the system dynamics, the instability spectrum is shaped into a stable cascade, a phenomenon governed by the real part of the Brillouin response. This establishes SBS as a controllable degree of freedom for managing nonlinear light propagation in Kerr resonators.
main_problem: The paper investigates how Stimulated Brillouin Scattering (SBS) influences Modulation Instability (MI) within Fiber Fabry-Perot (FFP) resonators.
main_result: SBS stabilizes the MI spectrum, shaping it into a stable multi-free-spectral-range cascade that would otherwise be unstable. This stabilization is attributed to the real part of the Brillouin response.
method: The study combines numerical simulations with experimental measurements using an FFP cavity, analyzing both spectral and time-domain dynamics.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Fiber Fabry-Perot resonator, modeled using a mean-field approach extended to incorporate the Brillouin response function. The dynamics are governed by the interplay between Kerr nonlinearity and SBS.
key_observables: MI sideband positions, spectral stability, time-domain pulse train characteristics (e.g., 1.28 GHz vs. 10.21 GHz), and reduction in instantaneous frequency fluctuations.
important_parameters: The relative position of the Brillouin frequency shift with respect to the cavity resonances (e.g., 8 FSR spacing) is critical for determining the system's stability regime.
main_assumptions: SBS suppression in the experiment is achieved using a phase modulator (PM), and time-domain dynamics require filtering side lobes from OSA/BOSA measurements.
figures_summary: Figures compare numerical and experimental spectra/time-domain evolution with and without SBS control, illustrating the transition from unstable MI to a stable Brillouin-MI cascade.
paper_structure: The paper develops the model, presents numerical simulations comparing SBS on/off, details the experimental setup and measurements, and concludes by analyzing the physical origin of the stabilization effect.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how a nonlinear wave interaction (SBS) can act as a stabilizing mechanism in a complex optical cavity system, offering control over nonlinear dynamics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Numerical simulations. (a) detuning scan-stop ap- plied to the pump. The right axis gives the round-trip number, matching the vertical axis of (b–e). Spectral (b,d) and temporal (c,e) evolutions of the cavity output intensity during the scan- stop depicted in (a), without (b,c) and with (d,e) SBS. The blue line pointed by an arrow in (b) and (d) shows the prediction of the position of the MI side lobe at threshold from theory ( [19]). The pump power is fixed at 137mW. Cavity parameters are given in Supplementary Table S1.

Fig. 2. Evolution of the MI spectrum with increasing phase modulation amplitude. (a) Full optical spectrum recorded with an OSA. (b–f) Zoom on the MI sideband centered at 750 GHz away from the pump measured with a BOSA for differ- ent RF powers applied to the PM: (b) phase modulation off, (c) 3 dBm, (d) 9 dBm, (e) 12 dBm, and (f) 25 dBm (respectively modulation amplitudes β = 0.281, 0.396, 0.560, 3.53 rad). In- creasing RF power progressively suppresses SBS.

Fig. 4. Experimental characterization of MI spectral stability with and without SBS. (a) Zoom on the time-domain beat sig- nal obtained by optically filtering the cavity output of the first MI sideband, with (pink) and without (blue) SBS. (b) Normal- ized instantaneous frequency fluctuations extracted from the beat signals, for both cases. (c) Normalized histograms of the instantaneous frequency fluctuations.

Fig. 3. Comparison of experimental and simulated MI spectra with and without phase modulation. Left column: steady-state output spectra (blue: experiment, pink: numerics) obtained af- ter the scan-stop procedure (a) without phase modulation and (c) with strong phase modulation suppressing SBS gain. Insets show a magnified view of the first MI sideband peak (black box). Right column: simulated spectral evolution during the scan-stop for the corresponding cases, (b) without and (d) with phase modulation.

(b–d) Typical spectral evolution (top) and final temporal profiles (bottom) obtained from identical scan-stop simulations for different SBS shift positions: (b) 8.05, (c) 8.5 and (d) 8.95 FSR.
